title: Salted Caramel Ice Cream
subtitle: Dry caramel custard ice cream with a deep, bitter-sweet edge and a salt finish
excerpt: A custard ice cream built from a dry caramel dissolved back into the milk, the result is a deeper, slightly bitter flavour that balances the richness of the cream and the salt. Watch the caramel closely once it starts to colour.
sourceNotes: Salted caramel became fashionable in British cooking in the mid-2000s, following its popularisation in French pâtisserie, particularly by chefs such as Henri Le Roux. The salted caramel ice cream, a custard base enriched with a dry caramel, is now a standard of the British artisan ice cream trade.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in an airtight container for up to 3 months. Press baking paper against the surface to prevent ice crystals.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The custard base can be made a day ahead and kept covered in the fridge before churning.

content.text: Salted caramel ice cream starts with a dry caramel. Cook sugar without water until it melts and darkens. Dissolve it back into hot milk, then use that as the base for the custard. The caramel adds a deep, slightly bitter note that balances the cream and the salt.

Scatter 80g caster sugar into a medium, heavy-based saucepan in a thin, even layer. Cook over a medium heat without stirring, swirl the pan gently if the sugar is melting unevenly, but do not stir. Watch closely: the sugar will melt from the edges inwards and turn from golden to a deep amber colour. As soon as it is a uniform deep amber (like dark treacle), remove from the heat immediately. Carefully pour the warm milk into the pan, it will spit and bubble furiously. Stir until the caramel has completely dissolved back into the milk. If lumps remain, return to a very low heat and stir until smooth.

Whisk the egg yolks and 100g caster sugar in a large heatproof bowl until pale and thick. Add the double cream to the caramel milk and heat together until just below boiling. Pour the hot caramel cream slowly onto the egg yolks, whisking constantly. Return to the saucepan over a low heat and stir continuously for 8 to 10 minutes until the custard thickens. Stir in the vanilla extract and the salt. Pour into a clean bowl, press cling film onto the surface, and cool completely. Refrigerate for at least 4 hours.

Taste the cold custard and adjust the salt if needed, the saltiness should be present but background, not dominant. Churn in an ice cream maker for 25 minutes until thick and softly set. Transfer to a freezer-safe container and freeze for at least 6 hours, or overnight.

items.symptom: Caramel burnt before it dissolved in the milk
items.cause: The caramel was taken too dark, or the heat was too high.
items.fix: A properly done dry caramel is a deep amber, stop just before it looks as dark as you want, as it continues cooking for a moment after the pan is off the heat. A slightly bitter note is correct and desirable; true burning gives an acrid, irredeemable flavour.

items.symptom: Caramel lumps remained in the milk
items.cause: The temperature difference between the caramel and milk was too great, causing the caramel to seize.
items.fix: Use warm milk rather than cold, this minimises the temperature shock. If lumps remain, return to a very low heat and stir gently until they dissolve.

items.cause: The salt was insufficient to balance the caramel and cream.
items.fix: Add another pinch of flaky salt to the churned ice cream. Fold it in gently when transferring to the container.

content.text: Keeps in the freezer for up to 3 months. Allow 5 minutes at room temperature before scooping.
